title: The martyrdom of Polycarp
hookLine: a martyr's account: the old bishop gives thanks before the fire
tomorrow: how would you pick a Christian out of a crowd? an old letter says…

lines: A ROAR YOU FEEL IN YOUR RIBS.
cards: A packed stadium has a roar you can feel in your ribs. An old man is led into one. The Roman governor, the proconsul, almost tries to help him.
Respect your age, he says. Swear by Caesar. Curse Christ, and I'll let you go.

The roar waits. The story of what happened next comes to us as a letter, from the church in Smyrna to other churches, so they would know how their bishop died. A gentle note: it ends in a death, told without detail.

teach.b: Over that roar, his answer is short: "Fourscore and six years have I been His servant, and He hath done me no wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?" Fourscore and six is eighty-six.
Some readers take it as his age, some as his years since baptism; the letter doesn't say. Notice what he doesn't say. Not I'm brave.

teach.h: NO WRONG IN ALL OF IT.
teach.b: He talks about a long friendship: someone I've served for a lifetime, who has never done me wrong. The letter keeps catching small, human sounds.

When soldiers came to arrest him, he had food and drink set out for them, and asked only for time to pray. At the end, they meant to nail him to the stake; he asked to be left as he was, and they tied him instead.
And then, tied, he looks up and prays aloud.
He blesses God for counting him worthy of this day and this hour. The fire is real, and the letter doesn't pretend otherwise.
But inside the loudest place of his life, the sound the letter keeps is quiet: before the hardest thing, Polycarp's first word is thank you.

how: Churches that keep a calendar of saints remember Polycarp on his feast day, and some read from the letter of the church at Smyrna that tells his story.

games.q: what does “the martyrdom of polycarp” mean?
o: the speech Polycarp wrote to defend himself in court
a festival where a city honored its oldest bishop
how an old bishop faced death, giving thanks first

games.q: the letter from Smyrna — tap the pairs.
p: the church that sent the letter
given food and drink by Polycarp
thanks, for this day and hour

s: Polycarp's last prayer was a plea to be rescued
the letter has him give thanks for being counted worthy of that day and hour.
the letter says 'fourscore and six' is his age
it doesn't say; some read his age, some his years since baptism.
Polycarp had food set out for the soldiers who came to arrest him
and asked only for time to pray.

games.q: your friend's mom has surgery tomorrow. at dinner the family is quiet and scared, and your friend asks you to say grace. with Polycarp's story in mind, what comes first?
o: thanks, for each other, before the hard day.
the worst cases, so everyone is ready.
nothing yet; thanks can wait till it's over.
games.why: before the fire, Polycarp gives thanks for a long friendship and for that very day. thanks first doesn't hide the hard thing; it walks in ahead of it.

practice: Bring to mind one hard thing waiting for you: a conversation, an appointment, a long shift. Before you think about how it will go, count three things to be thankful for inside it or around it, one finger at a time.
Then rest your hand and stay with that thanks for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The martyrdom of Polycarp. The letter from Smyrna telling how an old bishop faced the fire, and gave thanks before it.

orig.note: Greek: a witness. The word that gives English 'martyr'.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: eighty-six years, a long friendship and no wrong done in all of it. Peace to you.
